brief.head: The unsolved heart
brief.text: A friend of Ajay Shah’s says the heart is a solved problem. Biologically, yes, Amit Varma replied, but metaphorically “no one can solve the heart.” {086-J17}

thought.text: The only thing that leads to human progress is rethinking the fundamentals.
thought.who: Amit Varma, setting out the theme, not long after his own angioplasty

lead.kicker: Amit Varma’s stent, and the rebels who made it possible
lead.head: Rebels with a catheter
body: Amit Varma came to the studio in a full-sleeve shirt, and after a joke about showing too much skin, explained why. Half his arm had been shaved for an angioplasty.

A few days earlier he had been told that he had had a minor heart attack, and had not noticed. A CT scan found an 80 to 90 per cent block in his right coronary artery. By the time of the procedure it was 100 per cent. {086-S01}

He had blamed dust, COVID and food poisoning for weeks of acidity, vomiting and a tight chest. “The way I imagine a heart attack is that there’s a dramatic moment, background music increases,” he said. “There was nothing dramatic.”
For Ajay Shah, it was personal. His father had a small heart attack in 1982 that was recognised as one only a month later. He died of a second in 1984, aged 58. {086-S03}
## Rethink, don’t polish

In hospital, Varma had been reading about DeepSeek, and a line from a thread by Morgan Brown gave him the episode: incumbents optimise existing processes, while disruptors rethink the fundamental approach.
“The only thing that leads to human progress is rethinking the fundamentals,” he said. “There’s absolutely nothing else.” {086-C01}
The people who do it, he said, are maligned and treated like heretics, above all by those Paul Graham calls the aggressively conventional minded.
Medicine supplied the first of them. In Berlin in 1929, Werner Forssmann, a 25-year-old doctor, guided a catheter into his own heart.

In Australia, Barry Marshall drank water laced with the bacterium behind stomach ulcers to prove they were an infection. Charles Dotter built catheters in his kitchen, and in 1977 Andreas Gruentzig performed the first coronary angioplasty.
## Cricket, couches and Bombay
Cricket supplied Sri Lanka, underdogs who won the 1996 World Cup by sending two lower-order batsmen to open and attack from the first ball.
Strategy lags a change of format by years or even decades, Varma argued, and even after a heretic is proved right, adoption is slow.

Business supplied Netflix, which beat Blockbuster by posting DVDs without late fees, then moved into streaming in 2007, before the technology seemed ready. Its reasoning, as Varma put it: “If we don’t do it, somebody else will, and our business will get over.” {086-S10}
Varma’s own story was of being too early. In 2000 he pitched New York investors what was “basically MySpace” and “basically iTunes”, from Bombay. Then the Nasdaq crashed. {086-S12}
Thinking outside the box, he concluded, is necessary but not sufficient. You also need luck, and the persistence to give it more chances.
## Breeding heretics

Ajay Shah asked where such disruptors come from, and answered with four pillars: a culture of irreverence, gatekeepers who reward novelty, a society that honours failure, and tolerance for people who are not nice. “More stifling societies just make stultified people,” he said.
Varma noted that Shah had thereby implied he was not a nice guy, a weirdo and one of the nutcases. He accepted all of it.
The hosts ended on machines. Varma quoted a reply to a question by the podcaster Dwarkesh Patel: “To an LLM, a novel discovery is indistinguishable from an error.”
The human edge, Varma said, is to dive into what is new without assuming that what has not been said before must be crap.

second.label: Medicine
second.head: He drank the evidence
second.deck: Ajay Shah on the Australian doctor who gave himself ulcers to prove their cause
body: Stomach ulcers were once treated as a degenerative disease of old age, like cholesterol, Ajay Shah said. There was no cure: only bland food and avoiding stress, and people died horrible deaths.

In Australia, Barry Marshall argued that ulcers were a simple infectious disease, and nobody accepted it. To meet Koch’s postulates, he experimented on himself: he scoped his own healthy stomach, drank water containing Helicobacter pylori and scoped again to show full-blown ulcers.

A simple course of antibiotics cleared them, which a third look confirmed. {086-S05} Marshall won the 2005 Nobel Prize for Medicine. {#nobel2005} “You need the genius mad men with conviction,” Amit Varma said.

quote.text: He deliberately took the bacteria into his own body and went through the course of antibiotics and it got cleared up.

photo.subject: Barry Marshall
photo.hint: Australian physician, Nobel laureate in medicine

second.caption: how stomach ulcers were solved

third.head: Fangs, but no fanfare
body: Heart attacks are not the only killers that come without drama. Ajay Shah offered the bite of a venomous snake as an analogy.
As a city child, he said, he imagined a cobra bite as a cataclysm: the fangs gripping your calf, and a few moments later you keel over dead.

In fact, he said, such snakes bite at high speed, pump venom in like a hypodermic syringe and get far away. {086-S02} The victim feels very little and may see only two puncture marks, while the drama plays out over minutes and hours. Victims of common krait bites are bitten in their sleep and found dead in the morning.
Amit Varma pictured the Shah and Thomas household at night, with Shah waking to ask, “Susan, did you bite me just now?” {086-J06}
third.caption: the snake bite you barely feel

sections.label: Medicine, part one
sections.head: Pac-Man in the arteries
sections.caption: the procedure he watched on three screens
body: Amit Varma explained his procedure before its history. Doctors made an insertion in the radial artery, put in a sheath and ran a guide wire all the way to the heart. Along it went a catheter, a thin tube that can carry dye or a balloon.
In his case the balloon carried a drug-eluting stent. The balloon expanded, the stent expanded with it, and the balloon came out, leaving the stent in place.

He lay beside three screens, like a day trader’s, while a doctor worked what was practically a video-game controller. “Like in a game of Pac-Man,” he said, they manoeuvred through his arteries zapping clots, then dealt with a block that had reached 100 per cent. {086-J16}
It was all over in an hour. “So miraculous,” he said.
## Nowhere near the heart
In 1929, Varma said, the conventional wisdom was to take a catheter nowhere near the heart. In a leg, where arteries are wider, the worst outcome was losing the leg. The heart was too sensitive.

Werner Forssmann, a 25-year-old doctor in Berlin, went ahead on himself. His boss at the next hospital, Ferdinand Sauerbruch, was Varma’s example of the aggressively conventional minded. {086-J15} The phrase is Paul Graham’s, for people to whom a challenge to convention feels like a personal affront. {086-C02}
~ Had Forssmann died on the table, Varma said, modern science would have got there anyway. “But we would not know the name of that dude.” {#noname}

quote.text: With such experiments you might habilitate in a circus, but these have no place in a decent German hospital.
quote.who: Ferdinand Sauerbruch, as quoted by Amit Varma

sections.label: Medicine, part two
sections.head: The plumber and the diplomat
sections.caption: two pioneers of angioplasty
body: Charles Dotter, who pioneered angioplasty in other parts of the body from the 1960s, was openly rebellious, Amit Varma said. He went to first principles: the heart is, after all, a physical object.
His favourite “conceptual trademark” was a sketch of a crossed pipe and wrench. If a plumber can do it to pipes, Dotter said, “we can do it to blood vessels.” {#plumber}
Varma used a distinction Ajay Shah once drew between technicians, trained in procedures, and thinkers, who question them. Dotter was both. {086-C03}
## Playing the system
Andreas Gruentzig, much younger, thought the same way with the opposite temperament. He knew you had to play the system and be polite to everyone. {086-S07}

Why open the heart for a bypass, he asked, when a catheter could carry a balloon to the blockage? Textbooks and top surgeons warned of ventricular fibrillation and death within minutes. In 1977 he went ahead, on around six patients, and his talk won a standing ovation. {#sixpatients}
Stents met the same resistance, because once one is in the heart it cannot be removed. They arrived in the 1980s and were routine by the mid-1990s.
~ Only partly insured, Varma saw his bill and imagined a perpetual heart attack machine. Shah diagnosed Zeno-phobia: “the irrational fear of convergent sequences”. {086-J07}

quote.text: Gruentzig is a guy who knows that you gotta play the system, that you gotta write the papers in the right order

sections.label: Sport
sections.head: Bang bang bang from ball one
sections.caption: Sri Lanka’s 1996 heresy
body: Sri Lanka came to the 1996 World Cup as underdogs, much like India in 1983. The example came to Amit Varma from Pranay Kotasthane.

The template of the day had openers build, the middle order consolidate and everyone slog in the last ten overs. With field restrictions making early boundaries more profitable, Sri Lanka sent two lower-order batsmen, Romesh Kaluwitharana and Sanath Jayasuriya, out to open and attack. They took the Cup. {086-S08}

Strategy is slow to catch up with a new format, Varma argued. When one-day cricket arrived, Sunil Gavaskar made 36 not out in a 60-over match at the 1975 World Cup, playing to Test rhythms. {#gavaskar}
## The price of a dot ball

In T20 the same eleven batsmen get only twenty overs. That raises the cost of a dot ball and lowers the cost of a wicket, so the expected value of aggression rises. {086-C05} Send the hitters out first, Varma said, and keep the anchor for emergencies.
England later applied the logic to one-day cricket, and 300-plus scores, once common mainly on the subcontinent’s flat pitches, became common everywhere. {#england300}
~ Around 2016 Varma told a poker friend who bet on cricket to back the team batting second in the IPL. After fourteen games, the chasing side had won thirteen. {#thirteen}

quote.text: We will ask them to open the innings and we will ask them to go bang bang bang from the start.

sections.label: Movies
sections.head: First Blockbuster, then itself
sections.caption: how Netflix disrupted itself
body: Amit Varma often criticises Netflix for what it does in India. Its origin story, he said, is a brilliant example of a company that disrupted others and was not disrupted itself.
In the late 1990s Blockbuster ruled American home video: a store with a limited collection, and late fees, “punishing the Bengali procrastinator”. {086-J11}

From 1997 Netflix posted DVDs with no late fees, soon on a monthly subscription, with a catalogue browsable on the web. Blockbuster dismissed it as a niche until Netflix had 4.2 million subscribers by 2004. {#subscribers}
## Streaming too soon
In 2007, when internet speeds and screens made streaming seem unfeasible, Netflix moved into it anyway. {086-S10}
Five or six years later came original shows such as *House of Cards*, with whole seasons dropped at once. Binge-watching became the norm.
Kodak, by contrast, saw digital photography coming and protected its market. BlackBerry was sure people wanted keyboards, and Nokia was disrupted too. {086-C07}
~ The conventional thinking about short attention spans is wrong, Varma said, pointing to the many comments on a ten-and-a-half-hour episode he recorded with Ajay Shah. {#tenhalf}

quote.text: But internally a big company is always doing the safe thing and protecting its market. And why would I disrupt myself?

sections.label: The four pillars
sections.head: Weirdos welcome
sections.caption: where disruptors come from
body: Where do disruptors come from? Ajay Shah offered four pillars.

The first is culture. Societies that regiment children and hound them into competitive exams produce conformists. Without a culture of irreverence, he said, “you’re just going to become a banker”. A more easygoing culture tolerates heretics. “Very many people will go off to the beaches of Goa and get doped out, but a small fraction of them will become amazing people.” {086-J12}
The second is the gatekeepers: allocators of venture capital, research funding, journal space, patents and licences. If editors reward conformism, researchers end up “polishing the apple”. {086-C11}
## Failure, and the weirdos
The third is to embrace survivorship bias. “You have to throw a hundred darts at society and two of them will work out,” Shah said. That does not make the two geniuses. {086-C12}

The fourth is that truly disruptive people are often not nice. {086-C13} Alexander Solzhenitsyn, up close, was not a good human being, Shah said, and had there been social media in Newton’s time, his writing would have looked cringeworthy.

~ Amit Varma added that Silicon Valley works partly because its culture makes it okay to fail. He praised Emergent Ventures for funding those whom conventional allocators miss: “the freaks” and “the nutcases”. {086-J14}

quote.text: So more stifling societies just make stultified people and we are less likely to get thinking from them.

sections.label: The machines
sections.head: Error, or eureka?
sections.caption: what language models cannot yet find
body: In the show’s second episode Ajay Shah had asked whether AI could come up with something as drastic as the theory of relativity. Amit Varma returned to the question.
The podcaster Dwarkesh Patel had asked why language models, with the entire corpus of human knowledge memorised, have not made a single new connection that led to a discovery. {086-R29}

A user called Michael replied: “To an LLM, a novel discovery is indistinguishable from an error.” Varma saw a grain of truth in it, but AI is not only LLMs, he said, and will one day make discoveries. {086-C15}
## Ajay Shah’s law

Shah offered a law: if an LLM can write it, it is not worth writing. {086-C16} He tried to get one to produce, from a one-paragraph prompt, a paper on why India’s FRBM failed. It could not, so the paper was worth writing.
Varma, a power user, pushed back. By Sturgeon’s law, he said, 95 per cent of everything is crap, so default output will be too. {086-J20} Used well, the tools are “mind blowing” for research.
~ Shah does use the paid Google Gemini. Asked to find flaws in a newspaper column, it gave five suggestions “like what a master editor would do”. {086-R32}

quote.text: If you can supply a prompt and the LLM can write the paper, then you should just publish it as the prompt.

side.boxText: Paul Graham’s essay *The Four Quadrants of Conformism* named the enemy: the aggressively conventional minded. The thesis came from a thread on DeepSeek by Morgan Brown, which Amit Varma read in hospital: “Incumbents optimize existing processes while disruptors rethink the fundamental approach.” {086-R02}

contQuote.text: Thinking outside the box is a necessary but not sufficient condition. You also need luck, but you also need persistence because that is how you increase your surface area of serendipity.

stories.caption: Werner Forssmann’s self-experiment
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the doctor who catheterised himself in 1929
stories.head: A man after his own heart
body: In Berlin in 1929, catheters had just come into use and early angiography of other organs had begun. {#berlin1929} But the conventional wisdom, Amit Varma said, was that you went nowhere near the heart.

Werner Forssmann, a 25-year-old doctor, believed a catheter could be taken into the heart. His superior forbade the experiment. Forssmann agreed with part of the caution: he would not put something in someone else’s heart. He would put it in his own. {086-S04}
His nurse, who was devoted to him, would not hear of it. He was too important, she said, and he should experiment on her instead.

He strapped her down and gave her a local anaesthetic. Then, while she waited, he slid the catheter into his own arm and guided it up the vein with a mirror. By the time she realised she had been duped, it was a done deal.
They walked to the X-ray lab, where, with a fluoroscope, he guided the catheter into the right atrium of his heart. He did it nine more times on himself, and lost his job. {#ninemore}

At the next hospital Ferdinand Sauerbruch sneered that such experiments belonged in a circus. By 1932, Varma said, Forssmann’s game was over and he had moved to urology. He joined the Nazi party and spent five years imprisoned after the war, a part of the story Varma called irrelevant, because he always separates art and artist.
~ Meanwhile, others went deeper into his work. In the 1950s Forssmann won a Nobel Prize. {#nobel} He died in 1979, at 75, of a heart attack.
stories.why: A procedure Amit Varma went through fully conscious in 2025 began with one young Berlin doctor betting his own body against the consensus, and paying for it with his career. Varma, who calls him Werner, feels close to him.
stories.postscript: Narendra Shenoy told Varma this story while he was in hospital. {#shenoy}

stories.caption: Charles Dotter and the borrowed blowtorch
stories.kicker: A salesman’s memory of Charles Dotter, as read by Amit Varma
stories.head: Lend me your blowtorch
body: At a conference in the early 1960s, Bill Cook, a travelling salesman, noticed a short, muscular, bald man with darting eyes sitting on a box behind his stall. He made Cook nervous.

Just before closing, the stranger asked to borrow Cook’s blowtorch and some Teflon tubing, to practise making catheters in his hotel room. Cook thought he had “a real space cadet” on his hands, but agreed, and asked his name. It was Charles Dotter, who often assembled catheters in his own kitchen. {#kitchen}

“The next morning he was waiting for me with ten beautifully made Teflon catheters and my blowtorch,” Cook recalled. {086-S06} They were sold that day for ten dollars each, and Cook called Dotter “my first production employee”.
~ Cook, who had just started his business, went on to found the leader in angioplasty equipment.
stories.why: Dotter was not just a thinker reasoning from first principles and trying to convince people, Amit Varma said. He was a doer, making the things himself and carrying out the experiments.

stories.caption: Sonictown, his start-up that came too early
stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s music start-up, pitched in New York in 2000
stories.head: Right idea, wrong year
body: In 1999, in his early twenties, Amit Varma was shown the godown of Magnasound, Shashi Gopal’s label behind Daler Mehndi, Alisha Chinai and Baba Sehgal. It held thousands of CDs, and Gopal told him to take what he wanted. {#godown}

Varma told him that in ten years they would be worthless, because all music would be digital and sold online. He convinced Gopal and Sunil Mengrajani, Gopal’s head of marketing, and the three became equal partners in Sonictown.
In the Napster era labels wanted to crush digital music. Even so, Mengrajani secured rights to 80,000 songs from American labels. {#tracks}
In early 2000, before a room of New York investors, Varma pitched online song sales and pages where musicians could connect and update fans. {086-S12} The room was excited. Then the Nasdaq crashed.
~ Business World gave it a double spread.

quote.text: I laid out what was basically MySpace and I laid out what was basically iTunes.

stories.postscript: A second venture later left Varma deeply in debt, which, he said, is a story for another time.

stories.caption: Govind Nihalani’s missing film
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Govind Nihalani and a film lost to inertia
stories.head: The director’s missing Party
body: Around 2010 the director Govind Nihalani wanted to film Amit Varma’s 2009 novel, a book Varma calls bad. Varma naively tried to talk him out of it, then helped write a treatment.
Nobody would fund it, though Nihalani had made *Ardh Satya* and *Tamas*. At his suggestion Varma set a version in Pune, for the Marathi industry. Then he lost touch, too embarrassed to reconnect.

Nihalani had once told him his one regret: he had no copy of his own film *Party*. {086-S11} Varma’s friend Ved Sharma in New York found it on Netflix, kept the disc, paid the charge and posted it. By then inertia had set in, and it never reached Nihalani.
~ Varma believes Nihalani got a copy elsewhere. Ajay Shah worried that in the meantime DVD players had vanished from the world. {#dvdplayers}
stories.why: Even a director of Nihalani’s stature could not get an independent film funded, Varma said. And Netflix’s catalogue held a film its maker could not find in his own country.

quiz.q: What test told Amit Varma that he had already had a minor heart attack?
quiz.a: An HS troponin test, for a protein the heart releases during an attack.

quiz.q: Why did Amit Varma spend a day or two in ICU before his stent?
quiz.a: He was allergic to aspirin, which he must take daily for life with a stent.

quiz.q: What did Barry Marshall drink to prove that stomach ulcers are an infectious disease?
quiz.a: Water containing Helicobacter pylori; then he cured the ulcers with a course of antibiotics.

quiz.a: In 2007, when internet speeds and screens were too poor for watching films.

quiz.a: If an LLM can write it from a prompt, it is not worth writing.
